title: Python for Networking
sub: Sockets, struct, threads and subprocess: write your own client, server, scanner and monitor
goals: Write a TCP echo server and client and explain why TCP is a byte stream
Send and receive UDP datagrams and see why silence is the only error you get
Parse a raw IPv4 and TCP header from hex with struct
Scan ports in parallel with threads and a connect timeout
Fetch web data with urllib, http.client and ssl, and drive ping and dig with subprocess
Build portscan.py, a scanner that refuses targets outside your own network

blocks.text: You will build a small collection of network programs from the bottom up: a server and a client that talk over loopback, a chat room, a threaded port scanner, a banner grabber, a raw HTTP client, a ping sweeper and an uptime monitor. Along the way you meet the same objects you used from the shell in [Ports and sockets](#ports) and [HTTP](#http), now from the programmer's side. Every tool you used earlier (`nc`, `curl`, `nmap`, `dig`) is a program that calls the same handful of functions you are about to call.

The in-page Python runner has no network access: browsers do not allow raw sockets. Programs that open sockets are shown as `file` blocks. Create them in PyCharm or with `nano`, and run them in your own Terminal. Code that only parses bytes and text (`struct`, `ipaddress`, `urllib.parse`, `re`) does run in the page, and those blocks have a Run button.

What a socket is

A **socket** is the kernel's endpoint for network communication. Your program asks the kernel for one with the `socket()` system call and gets back a file descriptor, the same kind of small integer as stdin and stdout from [Streams and pipes](#pipes). Reading and writing that descriptor moves bytes to and from the network. The kernel does the protocol work: segmenting, retransmitting, acknowledging, ordering.
Two choices define a socket when you create it:

head: Choice
Values
Meaning
rows: IPv4, IPv6, or a local file path (no network)
TCP (reliable byte stream) or UDP (independent datagrams)

blocks.text: The server uses **two kinds of socket**. The listening socket only accepts new connections. Each `accept()` returns a brand-new connected socket (`conn`) for one client, plus the client's address. That is how one port serves many clients at once: the kernel tells connections apart by the full 4-tuple of source address, source port, destination address and destination port.

blocks.title: bind, listen, accept are separate on purpose

blocks.text: `bind` attaches an address to the socket. `listen` marks it passive and sets up the kernel queue of half-open and completed handshakes (the **backlog**). `accept` pulls one finished handshake off that queue. Separating them lets a server bind a privileged or well-known port, drop its privileges, and only then start accepting.

blocks.name: socket.socket()
blocks.sum: Create a socket object for a chosen address family and type.

how.text: The call wraps the `socket(2)` system call and returns an object that owns a file descriptor. Use it as a context manager (`with socket.socket() as s:`) so the descriptor is closed even when an exception happens. The defaults give a TCP socket over IPv4.
`SOCK_DGRAM` selects UDP. For IPv6 use `AF_INET6`; for a dual-stack client prefer `socket.create_connection()`, which tries every address a name resolves to.

examples.desc: Open and close a TCP socket, and inspect it
examples.code: python3 -c 'import socket; s = socket.socket(); print(s.family, s.type, s.fileno()); s.close()'

examples.desc: List the socket type constants Python knows, sorted
examples.code: python3 -c 'import socket; print(*[n for n in dir(socket) if n.startswith("SOCK_")], sep="\n")' | sort

gotchas: A socket you forget to close keeps its descriptor and, for a listener, its port. Always use `with`.

blocks.name: socket.bind()
blocks.sum: Attach a local address and port to a socket so clients can reach it.

how.text: The argument is one tuple for IPv4: the address and the port. `"127.0.0.1"` accepts connections only from this machine. `""` or `"0.0.0.0"` accepts them on every interface, which exposes the service to your whole LAN. Port 0 asks the kernel to pick a free port, and `sock.getsockname()` tells you which one.
Ports below 1024 are privileged on many systems; macOS lets ordinary users bind low ports on all interfaces since Mojave, but do not rely on it elsewhere. Use ports above 1024 for experiments.

examples.desc: Let the kernel choose a free port
examples.code: python3 -c 'import socket; s = socket.socket(); s.bind(("127.0.0.1", 0)); print(s.getsockname())'

examples.desc: Ask for three free ports and sort them
examples.code: for i in 1 2 3; do python3 -c 'import socket; s=socket.socket(); s.bind(("127.0.0.1", 0)); print(s.getsockname()[1])'; done | sort -n

gotchas: `OSError: [Errno 48] Address already in use` (Linux: 98) means another socket holds the port, or a recent connection lingers in TIME_WAIT. Check with `lsof -nP -iTCP:9000`, and set `SO_REUSEADDR` (below) for the TIME_WAIT case.

blocks.name: socket.listen()
blocks.sum: Mark a bound socket as passive so the kernel accepts connections for it.

how.text: After `listen()` the socket is in the LISTEN state and the kernel completes TCP handshakes on its behalf. Finished connections wait in a queue until your code calls `accept()`. `backlog` caps that queue; the default is a sensible system value, so you rarely pass it.

examples.desc: See the LISTEN state from another Terminal tab
examples.code:
python3 -c 'import socket,time; s=socket.socket(); s.bind(("127.0.0.1",9100)); s.listen(); time.sleep(30)' &
lsof -nP -iTCP:9100 -sTCP:LISTEN

examples.desc: Kill the background listener by port
examples.code: kill $(lsof -tiTCP:9100 -sTCP:LISTEN)

blocks.name: socket.accept()
blocks.sum: Wait for a client and return a new connected socket plus the client's address.

how.text: `accept()` blocks until a completed handshake is in the queue, then returns a new socket bound to that one conversation and the peer's `(ip, port)`. The listening socket stays open. A server loop is `while True: conn, addr = srv.accept()`, followed by handling the client inline (one at a time) or in a thread (many at once).

examples.desc: Accept one connection, then stop
examples.code: python3 -c 'import socket; s=socket.socket(); s.bind(("127.0.0.1",9101)); s.listen(); c,a=s.accept(); print("from",a)'

examples.desc: Connect to it from another tab with nc

gotchas: A blocked `accept()` ignores everything else your program wants to do. Use threads, `settimeout()` or `selectors` when the server must also watch for shutdown.

blocks.name: socket.connect()
blocks.sum: Open a TCP connection to a remote address.

how.text: The kernel sends a SYN, waits for SYN-ACK and completes the handshake. `connect` blocks until that finishes, fails with `ConnectionRefusedError` (an RST came back: nothing listens there), or hits the socket's timeout (no answer at all, often a firewall dropping packets). Those two failures look different on the wire and in code, and the difference is the basis of port scanning.

examples.desc: Connect to a local listener
examples.code: python3 -c 'import socket; s=socket.socket(); s.settimeout(2); s.connect(("127.0.0.1", 9000)); print("connected")'

examples.desc: Keep only the last line of the traceback when nothing listens
examples.code: python3 -c 'import socket; s=socket.socket(); s.settimeout(2); s.connect(("127.0.0.1", 9000))' 2>&1 | tail -n 1

gotchas: `connect(("example.com", 80))` resolves the name for you but only tries the first IPv4 address. Prefer `socket.create_connection()`.

blocks.name: socket.create_connection()
blocks.sum: Resolve a name and connect to the first address that works, IPv4 or IPv6.

how.text: The function calls `getaddrinfo()` and tries each result in order until one connects, so a host with both AAAA and A records works even when one family is broken. The `timeout` applies to the connect and stays set on the returned socket for later `recv()` calls.

examples.desc: Connect with a 3 second timeout and print the peer
examples.code: python3 -c 'import socket; s = socket.create_connection(("example.com", 80), timeout=3); print(s.getpeername()); s.close()'

examples.desc: Take the target from stdin and show both ends of the connection (start python3 -m http.server 8000 --bind 127.0.0.1 first)
examples.code: printf '127.0.0.1 8000\n' | python3 -c 'import socket,sys; h,p=sys.stdin.read().split(); s=socket.create_connection((h,int(p)),timeout=3); print(s.getsockname(),"->",s.getpeername())'

blocks.name: socket.sendall()
blocks.sum: Send all of a bytes object, retrying until the kernel has taken every byte.

how.text: `send()` may accept fewer bytes than you offered (it returns how many it took). `sendall()` loops until everything is queued or an error occurs, so it is the right default for TCP. It queues data in the kernel's send buffer: it returning does not mean the peer has read the data.
Sockets carry **bytes**. Encode text first: `"hello".encode()` gives UTF-8 bytes, and `b"hello"` is a literal.

examples.desc: Send a message (the peer must be listening)
examples.code: python3 -c 'import socket; s=socket.create_connection(("127.0.0.1", 9000)); s.sendall("hello\n".encode()); s.close()'

examples.desc: Send whatever arrives on stdin (listen first with nc -l 127.0.0.1 9000)
examples.code: printf 'hello\n' | python3 -c 'import socket,sys; s=socket.create_connection(("127.0.0.1",9000)); s.sendall(sys.stdin.buffer.read()); s.close()'

gotchas: `s.sendall("text")` raises `TypeError: a bytes-like object is required`. Encode first.

blocks.name: socket.recv()
blocks.sum: Read up to a maximum number of bytes from a socket.

how.text: `recv(4096)` blocks until at least one byte is available, then returns between 1 and 4096 bytes. It never promises a whole message. An **empty bytes object `b""` means the peer closed its sending side**; it is not an error and it is how every read loop ends.
If a timeout is set and nothing arrives in time, `recv` raises `TimeoutError` (`socket.timeout` is an alias of it).

examples.desc: Read everything until the peer closes
examples.code:
python3 -c 'import socket; s=socket.create_connection(("127.0.0.1", 8000)); s.sendall(b"HEAD / HTTP/1.0\r\n\r\n"); b=b""
while c:=s.recv(4096): b+=c
print(b.decode()[:60])'

examples.desc: Count the bytes of a whole response (start python3 -m http.server 8000 --bind 127.0.0.1 first)
examples.code: python3 -c 'import socket,sys; s=socket.create_connection(("127.0.0.1",8000)); s.sendall(b"GET / HTTP/1.0\r\n\r\n"); [sys.stdout.buffer.write(c) for c in iter(lambda: s.recv(4096), b"")]' | wc -c

gotchas: Treating one `recv()` as one message works on loopback with tiny messages and fails on real networks. See the framing section.

blocks.name: socket.settimeout()
blocks.sum: Set how long blocking socket calls may wait.

how.text: `None` (the default) blocks forever. A number makes `connect`, `accept`, `recv` and `send` raise `TimeoutError` after that many seconds. `0.0` puts the socket in non-blocking mode, where calls that cannot finish at once raise `BlockingIOError`. A scanner needs a short timeout (0.3 to 1 second on a LAN) or one filtered port stalls a worker for minutes.

examples.desc: A connect that gives up after half a second
examples.code:
python3 -c 'import socket; s=socket.socket(); s.settimeout(0.5)
print(s.connect_ex(("192.168.1.250", 80)))'

examples.desc: Show only the exception a silent peer produces
examples.code: python3 -c 'import socket; l=socket.socket(); l.bind(("127.0.0.1",0)); l.listen(); s=socket.create_connection(l.getsockname()); s.settimeout(0.5); s.recv(10)' 2>&1 | tail -n 1

blocks.name: socket.connect_ex()
blocks.sum: Like connect(), but return an error number instead of raising an exception.

how.text: Returns `0` on success and a non-zero `errno` otherwise: `ECONNREFUSED` (61 on macOS, 111 on Linux) when a closed port answered with RST, and a timeout or `EHOSTUNREACH` code when nothing answered or the network said no route. That makes it a compact open-port test with no `try`.

examples.desc: Test one port
examples.code: python3 -c 'import socket; s=socket.socket(); s.settimeout(1); print("open" if s.connect_ex(("127.0.0.1", 8000)) == 0 else "closed")'

examples.desc: Sweep a few loopback ports from seq and keep the open ones
examples.code: seq 8000 8003 | python3 -c 'import socket,sys; [print(p, "open" if socket.socket().connect_ex(("127.0.0.1", int(p))) == 0 else "closed") for p in sys.stdin.read().split()]' | grep open

gotchas: Pass an IP address. If you pass a name that fails to resolve it still raises `socket.gaierror`.

blocks.name: socket.sendto() recvfrom()
blocks.sum: Send and receive single UDP datagrams, each tagged with an address.

how.text: A UDP socket has no connection. `sendto` addresses each datagram separately, and `recvfrom` returns one whole datagram together with the sender's `(ip, port)`. Datagram boundaries are preserved (unlike TCP), but delivery, order and even arrival are not guaranteed. If nobody listens, `sendto` still succeeds; you learn about the problem only by timing out.

examples.desc: Send a datagram to a port where nothing listens, and wait
examples.code: python3 -c 'import socket; s=socket.socket(socket.AF_INET, socket.SOCK_DGRAM); s.settimeout(1); s.sendto(b"hi", ("127.0.0.1", 9999)); print(s.recvfrom(100))'

examples.desc: Send stdin as a datagram to your own loopback receiver and read it back
examples.code: printf 'ping' | python3 -c 'import socket,sys; r=socket.socket(socket.AF_INET, socket.SOCK_DGRAM); r.bind(("127.0.0.1",0)); s=socket.socket(socket.AF_INET, socket.SOCK_DGRAM); s.sendto(sys.stdin.buffer.read(), r.getsockname()); print(r.recvfrom(100))'

gotchas: A socket you have not `connect()`ed never reports ICMP port unreachable, so a missing listener looks like a timeout. If you call `connect()` on the UDP socket first (which only sets a default peer), the error does surface as `ConnectionRefusedError` on the next `send` or `recv`.

blocks.name: socket.getaddrinfo()
blocks.sum: Resolve a host name and port into ready-to-use socket addresses, IPv4 and IPv6.
blocks.syntax: socket.getaddrinfo(host, port, family=0, type=0, proto=0, flags=0) -> list

how.text: This is the portable name resolver, the one browsers and `curl` use through the C library. It consults `/etc/hosts`, the macOS resolver and DNS in the order the system defines, and returns one 5-tuple per usable address: `(family, type, proto, canonname, sockaddr)`. Pass `family=socket.AF_INET` to keep only IPv4. `sockaddr` is `(ip, port)` for IPv4 and a 4-tuple for IPv6.
The older `socket.gethostbyname(name)` returns a single IPv4 string and `socket.gethostname()` returns your own machine's name. Prefer `getaddrinfo`.

examples.desc: List the addresses for a name
examples.code: python3 -c 'import socket; print(sorted({i[4][0] for i in socket.getaddrinfo("example.com", 443, proto=socket.IPPROTO_TCP)}))'

examples.desc: Resolve every name in hosts.txt

gotchas: Failures raise `socket.gaierror`; its `.strerror` is the message. This is not `dig`: it follows system policy, so `/etc/hosts` entries and per-domain VPN resolvers apply.

blocks.name: socket.setsockopt()
blocks.sum: Change a socket option at the socket or protocol level.

how.text: The one every server needs is `SO_REUSEADDR`. After a server stops, its closed connections sit in TIME_WAIT for up to a couple of minutes, and without the option `bind` on the same port fails with "Address already in use". With the option, `bind` succeeds as long as no socket is actually listening. It does not let two live listeners share a port.

examples.desc: Set the option before bind() so a restarted server can reuse its port
examples.code: python3 -c 'import socket; s=socket.socket(); s.setsockopt(socket.SOL_SOCKET, socket.SO_REUSEADDR, 1); s.bind(("127.0.0.1", 9000)); print("bound")'

examples.desc: Look for lingering connections that cause the error
examples.code: netstat -an -p tcp | grep -c TIME_WAIT

blocks.name: socket.makefile()
blocks.sum: Wrap a socket in a file object so you can read it line by line.

how.text: The wrapper adds buffering and decoding, so `for line in f:` yields one complete newline-terminated line at a time even when the bytes arrive in odd pieces. This is the easiest fix for line-oriented protocols (chat, SMTP, redis-like command sets).

examples.desc: Read a server's lines (start `python3 -m http.server 8000 --bind 127.0.0.1` first)
examples.code: python3 -c 'import socket; s=socket.create_connection(("127.0.0.1", 8000)); s.sendall(b"GET / HTTP/1.0\r\n\r\n"); print(s.makefile("r", encoding="utf-8").readline().rstrip())'

examples.desc: Print every response line, then keep only the Content headers
examples.code: python3 -c 'import socket; s=socket.create_connection(("127.0.0.1", 8000)); s.sendall(b"GET / HTTP/1.0\r\n\r\n"); [print(l.rstrip()) for l in s.makefile("r", encoding="utf-8")]' | grep -i content-

gotchas: Write and flush explicitly if you use a `"w"` file; mixing `makefile` reads with direct `recv()` on the same socket loses buffered data.

blocks.text: A TCP echo server and client
The smallest useful network program: the server sends back whatever it receives. Create `echo_server.py`:

blocks.code:
import socket

HOST, PORT = "127.0.0.1", 9000

with socket.socket(socket.AF_INET, socket.SOCK_STREAM) as srv:
    srv.setsockopt(socket.SOL_SOCKET, socket.SO_REUSEADDR, 1)
    srv.bind((HOST, PORT))
    srv.listen()
    print(f"listening on {HOST}:{PORT}", flush=True)
    while True:
        conn, addr = srv.accept()
        with conn:
            print("connection from", addr, flush=True)
            while True:
                data = conn.recv(4096)
                if not data:          # empty bytes: the peer closed its side
                    break
                conn.sendall(data)
            print("closed", addr, flush=True)

blocks.text: Walk through what each line asks the kernel to do:

blocks.title: The server side of a TCP conversation

tokens.exp: allow rebinding while old connections sit in TIME_WAIT
enter LISTEN; the kernel now completes handshakes
block until a client arrives, get a per-client socket
read 1 to 4096 bytes; b"" means the client finished
queue the same bytes for the way back

blocks.text: Now the client, `echo_client.py`:

blocks.code:
import socket
import sys

HOST, PORT = "127.0.0.1", 9000
message = " ".join(sys.argv[1:]) or "hello"

with socket.create_connection((HOST, PORT), timeout=3) as s:
    s.sendall(message.encode())
    s.shutdown(socket.SHUT_WR)        # tell the server we are done sending
    reply = b""
    while chunk := s.recv(4096):
        reply += chunk
print("sent    :", message)
print("received:", reply.decode())

blocks.text: `shutdown(SHUT_WR)` sends a FIN: it half-closes the connection so the server's `recv` returns `b""` and the server finishes, while the client can still read the reply. Without it, the client's read loop would wait for a close that the server only performs after it sees one from the client.
Tab 1: `python3 echo_server.py`. Tab 2: `python3 echo_client.py hello there`.

blocks.code:
$ python3 echo_server.py
listening on 127.0.0.1:9000
connection from ('127.0.0.1', 51342)
closed ('127.0.0.1', 51342)

$ python3 echo_client.py hello there
sent    : hello there
received: hello there

blocks.text: While the server runs, open a third tab and look at it from the outside, then talk to it with `nc` instead of your client:

blocks.code:
lsof -nP -iTCP:9000
echo "typed with nc" | nc -N 127.0.0.1 9000

blocks.text: macOS ships BSD `nc`. With data piped in, it can stay open waiting for the server to close; the `-N` flag (shut down the network socket after EOF) ends it when input ends on current macOS. If `-N` is rejected on your version, press [[Ctrl+C]] after the reply appears, or use `nc -w 1`.

blocks.title: Server handles one client at a time

blocks.text: The loop calls `accept()` again only after the current client finishes. Open `nc 127.0.0.1 9000` in tab 2 and leave it idle, then run the echo client from tab 3: it connects (the kernel completes the handshake) but gets no reply until you close the `nc`. Threads fix this, in the chat server below.
TCP is a stream, not a list of messages

If the client calls `sendall(b"HELO")` and then `sendall(b"scan 80")`, the server's `recv()` may return `b"HELOscan 80"`, or `b"HEL"` then `b"Oscan 80"`, or the two messages separately. TCP guarantees the **order and content of the bytes**, not where `send` boundaries fall. Loopback with small messages often looks message-oriented, which hides the bug until the network is real.
You must put message boundaries in the data. The two common ways:

items.text: **Delimiter**: end each message with `\n`. `makefile()` or `splitlines` then recovers them. Used by HTTP headers, SMTP, chat.
**Length prefix**: send the length first, then the payload. Used by TLS records, DNS over TCP (2-byte length), most binary protocols.

blocks.text: This block rebuilds messages from arbitrary chunks. It uses a 2-byte big-endian length (`!H`), exactly as DNS over TCP does. It runs in the page:

blocks.code:
import struct

# Three messages sent with sendall() can arrive as any number of recv() chunks.
stream = b"".join(struct.pack("!H", len(m)) + m for m in (b"HELO", b"scan 80,443", b"BYE"))
print(stream)

chunks = [stream[:3], stream[3:11], stream[11:]]      # arbitrary splits, like TCP segments
buf, messages = b"", []
for chunk in chunks:
    buf += chunk
    while len(buf) >= 2:
        (n,) = struct.unpack("!H", buf[:2])
        if len(buf) < 2 + n:
            break                                      # wait for more bytes
        messages.append(buf[2:2 + n])
        buf = buf[2 + n:]
print(messages)

blocks.text: The loop waits (`break`) when a message is incomplete and keeps leftover bytes in `buf`. That `buf` is the part beginners forget.
struct: packing numbers into bytes

Protocol headers are fixed layouts of integers. The `struct` module converts between Python numbers and those raw bytes. A **format string** describes the layout: one character per field, with a first character that selects byte order.

head: Char
Meaning
Size
rows: byte order: network (big-endian), the order headers use
byte order: little-endian (x86 and Apple Silicon memory order)

blocks.text: **Big-endian** means the most significant byte comes first: port 80 is `00 50`. Apple Silicon is little-endian, so Python's native packing would give `50 00`. Always start a wire format with `!`. A `!` format also turns off alignment padding, which is what you want for headers.

blocks.code:
import struct

data = struct.pack("!HHI", 80, 443, 3_000_000_000)
print(data, len(data))
print(struct.unpack("!HHI", data))
print(struct.pack("<H", 80), struct.pack(">H", 80))
print(struct.calcsize("!BBHHHBBH4s4s"), "bytes in a basic IPv4 header")
blocks.out:
b'\x00P\x01\xbb\xb2\xd0^\x00' 8
(80, 443, 3000000000)
b'P\x00' b'\x00P'
20 bytes in a basic IPv4 header

blocks.name: struct.pack()
blocks.sum: Convert Python values into bytes following a format string.

how.text: The format decides the size and byte order of each field. Values that do not fit raise `struct.error` (for example 70000 into `H`). The result is a bytes object ready for `sendall()` or a raw packet.

examples.desc: Build a 2-byte length prefix
examples.code:
import struct
print(struct.pack("!H", 513))

examples.desc: Write the packed bytes to stdout and view them in hex
examples.code: python3 -c 'import struct,sys; sys.stdout.buffer.write(struct.pack("!HH", 80, 443))' | od -An -tx1

blocks.name: struct.unpack()
blocks.sum: Convert bytes into a tuple of Python values following a format string.

how.text: The buffer length must equal `struct.calcsize(format)` exactly, otherwise `struct.error` is raised. To read a header out of a longer packet, slice first (`raw[:20]`) or use `struct.unpack_from(fmt, buf, offset)`. The result is always a tuple, even for one field: write `(n,) = struct.unpack("!H", b)`.

examples.desc: Read a port number from two bytes
examples.code:
import struct
(port,) = struct.unpack("!H", bytes([0x01, 0xBB]))
print(port)

examples.desc: Unpack two raw bytes sent through a pipe
examples.code: printf '\001\273' | python3 -c 'import struct,sys; print(struct.unpack("!H", sys.stdin.buffer.read())[0])'

gotchas: Forgetting `!` reads multi-byte fields in your CPU's order, so `00 50` becomes 20480 instead of 80.

blocks.text: Parse a raw IPv4 and TCP header

Packets from `tcpdump -x` or a capture show up as hex. With `struct` you can take a header apart yourself, which is the best way to learn what a header contains. The block below parses a TCP SYN packet as it would appear on the wire, 40 bytes: a 20-byte IPv4 header followed by a 20-byte TCP header. It also computes the **Internet checksum**: the 16-bit ones' complement of the ones' complement sum of all 16-bit words in the header.

blocks.code:
import struct
import ipaddress

HEX = (
    "45000028 1c464000 40060000 c0a80117 5db8d822"   # IPv4 header, 20 bytes (checksum zeroed)
    "c3a50050 00000001 00000000 5002ffff 00000000"   # TCP header, 20 bytes (SYN)
)
raw = bytes.fromhex(HEX)

ver_ihl, tos, total_len, ident, flags_frag, ttl, proto, csum, src, dst = \
    struct.unpack("!BBHHHBBH4s4s", raw[:20])
version, ihl = ver_ihl >> 4, ver_ihl & 0x0F
print(f"version={version} header={ihl * 4} bytes total_length={total_len}")
print(f"id={ident:#06x} DF={bool(flags_frag & 0x4000)} MF={bool(flags_frag & 0x2000)} "
      f"frag_offset={flags_frag & 0x1FFF}")
print(f"ttl={ttl} protocol={proto} ({'TCP' if proto == 6 else '?'})")
print("src", ipaddress.ip_address(src), "dst", ipaddress.ip_address(dst))

tcp = raw[ihl * 4:]
sport, dport, seq, ack, off_flags, window, tcsum, urg = struct.unpack("!HHIIHHHH", tcp[:20])
names = ["FIN", "SYN", "RST", "PSH", "ACK", "URG"]
flags = [n for i, n in enumerate(names) if off_flags & (1 << i)]
print(f"tcp {sport} -> {dport} seq={seq} ack={ack} header={(off_flags >> 12) * 4} bytes "
      f"flags={'|'.join(flags)} window={window}")


def checksum(header):
    """Internet checksum: ones' complement of the ones' complement sum of 16-bit words."""
    total = sum(struct.unpack(f"!{len(header) // 2}H", header))
    while total > 0xFFFF:
        total = (total & 0xFFFF) + (total >> 16)
    return ~total & 0xFFFF


good = checksum(raw[:20])
print(f"checksum to store in the header: {good:#06x}")
filled = raw[:10] + struct.pack("!H", good) + raw[12:20]
print("verifies (checksum over the filled header is 0):", checksum(filled) == 0)

id=0x1c46 DF=True MF=False frag_offset=0
ttl=64 protocol=6 (TCP)
src 192.168.1.23 dst 93.184.216.34

blocks.text: Match each printed value to the hex: `45` is version 4 with header length 5 words (5 x 4 = 20 bytes), `4000` has the DF (don't fragment) bit set, `40` is TTL 64, `06` is TCP, `c0a80117` is 192.168.1.23. In the TCP half `c3a5` is port 50085, `0050` is port 80, and `5002` is data offset 5 plus the SYN flag in the low bits. `ihl` and the TCP data offset are counted in 32-bit words, so multiply by 4 to get bytes.

blocks.title: Change one byte, see what moves

blocks.text: Change `40` (TTL) to `01`, or change the flags `5002` to `5012` (SYN+ACK) and re-run. The checksum changes when header bytes change, because it covers all of them. Then set the protocol byte `06` to `11` and note what the program claims.

blocks.title: Why the checksum check ends in zero

blocks.text: Ones' complement addition makes the checksum self-verifying: if the stored checksum is included in the sum, the final complement is 0 for an intact header. Routers decrement TTL, so they recompute the checksum at every hop. Modern hardware offloads checksums to the NIC, which is why packets captured on the sending host often show an incorrect checksum.
UDP: datagrams with no connection

UDP has no handshake, no retransmission and no stream. Each `sendto` becomes one datagram and each `recvfrom` returns one. Create `udp_time.py`, which is both a server (`serve`) and a client (default):

blocks.code:
import socket
import sys
from datetime import datetime, timezone

HOST, PORT = "127.0.0.1", 9001

def serve():
    with socket.socket(socket.AF_INET, socket.SOCK_DGRAM) as s:
        s.bind((HOST, PORT))
        print(f"udp time server on {HOST}:{PORT}", flush=True)
        while True:
            data, addr = s.recvfrom(1024)
            print("request from", addr, data, flush=True)
            now = datetime.now(timezone.utc).isoformat(timespec="seconds")
            s.sendto(now.encode(), addr)

def ask():
    with socket.socket(socket.AF_INET, socket.SOCK_DGRAM) as s:
        s.settimeout(2)
        s.sendto(b"time?", (HOST, PORT))
        try:
            data, _ = s.recvfrom(1024)
        except socket.timeout:
            sys.exit("no reply (UDP gives no error, only silence)")
        print("server says:", data.decode())

if __name__ == "__main__":
    serve() if sys.argv[1:] == ["serve"] else ask()

UDP never tells the sender that nobody is listening; DNS clients, for example, rely on timeouts and retries for exactly this reason. Compare with `nc -u -z 127.0.0.1 9001` and with the UDP rows of `nmap -sU`, which are always slower than TCP scans.
Threads: serving many clients

A blocking `accept()` or `recv()` freezes the whole thread. Threads give each client its own flow of control. In CPython the Global Interpreter Lock lets only one thread run Python bytecode at a time, but a thread blocked in a socket call releases the lock, so threads are an excellent fit for **I/O-bound** work such as chat servers and port scanners. They are a poor fit for CPU-heavy loops.

blocks.name: threading.Thread
blocks.sum: Run a function in a separate thread of control.

how.text: `start()` begins execution; `join()` waits for it to end. A **daemon** thread is killed when the main thread exits, which is what you want for per-client handlers in a server. Threads share memory, so two threads changing the same dict or list need a `threading.Lock` (`with lock:`) around the update, or the program works on most runs and corrupts data on some.

blocks.text: Here is a threaded chat server. The shared `clients` dict is protected by a lock, each connection runs in its own daemon thread, and `makefile()` yields whole lines. Create `chat_server.py`:

blocks.code:
import socket
import threading

HOST, PORT = "127.0.0.1", 9002
clients = {}                     # socket -> nickname
lock = threading.Lock()

def broadcast(text, sender=None):
    data = (text + "\n").encode()
    with lock:
        for sock in list(clients):
            if sock is not sender:
                try:
                    sock.sendall(data)
                except OSError:
                    clients.pop(sock, None)

def handle(conn, addr):
    with conn, conn.makefile("r", encoding="utf-8", newline="\n") as lines:
        conn.sendall(b"nickname? ")
        nick = (lines.readline().strip() or f"{addr[0]}:{addr[1]}")[:20]
        with lock:
            clients[conn] = nick
        broadcast(f"* {nick} joined", conn)
        for line in lines:                       # one iteration per newline-terminated message
            broadcast(f"{nick}: {line.rstrip()}", conn)
    with lock:
        clients.pop(conn, None)
    broadcast(f"* {nick} left")

def main():
    with socket.socket() as srv:
        srv.setsockopt(socket.SOL_SOCKET, socket.SO_REUSEADDR, 1)
        srv.bind((HOST, PORT))
        srv.listen()
        print(f"chat on {HOST}:{PORT}", flush=True)
        while True:
            conn, addr = srv.accept()
            threading.Thread(target=handle, args=(conn, addr), daemon=True).start()

main()

hello bob

blocks.title: A shared dict needs a lock

concurrent.futures and the port scanner

A scan sends one connection attempt per port. Sequentially, 1,024 ports with a 0.5 second timeout on a host that drops packets takes over eight minutes. In parallel, 100 workers finish in about five seconds, because almost all of the time is waiting.

blocks.name: concurrent.futures.ThreadPoolExecutor
blocks.sum: Run many calls on a pool of worker threads and collect their results.

how.text: `pool.map(fn, items)` returns results in **input order**, even when workers finish out of order, and re-raises a worker's exception when you reach that result. `submit` returns a `Future`; `concurrent.futures.as_completed(futures)` yields futures as they finish, which suits progress output. The `with` block waits for all work and shuts the pool down. The default `max_workers` is `min(32, cpu_count + 4)`; for network waiting you can safely set 50 to 200, bounded by the open-files limit (`ulimit -n`, 256 by default in a macOS Terminal).

Banners, raw HTTP and TLS
Banner grabber

Many services announce themselves as soon as you connect (SSH, SMTP, FTP). Others, like HTTP, wait for a request. This grabber reads first and, if nothing arrives within two seconds, sends a minimal HTTP `HEAD`. Create `banner.py`:

import socket
import sys

with socket.create_connection((host, port), timeout=3) as s:
    s.settimeout(2)

HTTP from raw sockets

HTTP/1.1 is text over TCP: a request line, headers, a blank line (`\r\n\r\n`), and an optional body. Writing the client by hand shows exactly what `curl -v` was displaying in [HTTP](#http). Create `rawhttp.py`:

blocks.code:
import socket
import sys

host = sys.argv[1] if len(sys.argv) > 1 else "example.com"
port = int(sys.argv[2]) if len(sys.argv) > 2 else 80
request = f"GET / HTTP/1.1\r\nHost: {host}\r\nConnection: close\r\nUser-Agent: rawhttp/1.0\r\n\r\n"

with socket.create_connection((host, port), timeout=5) as s:
    s.sendall(request.encode("ascii"))
    chunks = []
    while chunk := s.recv(4096):
        chunks.append(chunk)

raw = b"".join(chunks)
head, _, body = raw.partition(b"\r\n\r\n")      # a blank line ends the headers
lines = head.decode("iso-8859-1").split("\r\n")
print("status line:", lines[0])
for line in lines[1:6]:
    print("header     :", line)
print("body bytes :", len(body))

$ python3 rawhttp.py example.com
status line: HTTP/1.1 200 OK
header     : Content-Type: text/html
header     : ETag: "3147526947+gzip"
header     : Age: 413217
header     : Cache-Control: max-age=604800
header     : Date: Thu, 08 Oct 2026 06:10:02 GMT
body bytes : 1256

blocks.text: `Connection: close` makes the server close after the response, so reading until `b""` captures all of it. Without it, HTTP/1.1 keeps the connection open and the loop would hang until the server's idle timeout. A real client needs `Content-Length` or chunked decoding to know where a response ends on a persistent connection, which is why you normally use a library.

One IP address serves many sites. The TCP connection carries only the address and port, so the `Host:` header is how the server picks the site. Remove it from `rawhttp.py` and most servers reply `400 Bad Request`, which makes a good break-it experiment.

The standard library covers ordinary HTTP without third-party packages. `urllib.parse` splits and builds URLs (it runs in the page); `urllib.request.urlopen` fetches; `http.client` gives control over methods and headers.

u = urlsplit("https://user@example.com:8443/api/v1/hosts?name=web+01&tag=a&tag=b#top")

blocks.text: To try both clients you need something to call. This tiny JSON API (`http.server`) answers `/time` and `/echo?...` and gives a 404 for anything else. Create `api_server.py`:

blocks.code:
import json
from datetime import datetime, timezone
from http.server import BaseHTTPRequestHandler, ThreadingHTTPServer
from urllib.parse import urlsplit, parse_qs

class Handler(BaseHTTPRequestHandler):
    def do_GET(self):
        url = urlsplit(self.path)
        if url.path == "/time":
            body = {"utc": datetime.now(timezone.utc).isoformat(timespec="seconds")}
            status = 200
        elif url.path == "/echo":
            body = {"query": parse_qs(url.query)}
            status = 200
        else:
            body, status = {"error": "not found", "path": url.path}, 404
        data = json.dumps(body).encode()
        self.send_response(status)
        self.send_header("Content-Type", "application/json")
        self.send_header("Content-Length", str(len(data)))
        self.end_headers()
        self.wfile.write(data)

    def log_message(self, fmt, *args):             # one tidy line per request, on stderr
        print(f"{self.address_string()} {fmt % args}", flush=True)

ThreadingHTTPServer(("127.0.0.1", 8080), Handler).serve_forever()

TLS with ssl

TLS wraps a TCP socket. `ssl.create_default_context()` builds a context that verifies the certificate chain against the system's trusted roots and checks that the certificate matches the host name. Pass the same name as `server_hostname` so SNI (which site you want) and verification both work. Create `cert_expiry.py`:

blocks.code:
import socket
import ssl
import sys
from datetime import datetime, timezone

host = sys.argv[1] if len(sys.argv) > 1 else "example.com"
ctx = ssl.create_default_context()            # verifies the chain and the host name
with socket.create_connection((host, 443), timeout=5) as raw:
    with ctx.wrap_socket(raw, server_hostname=host) as tls:
        cert = tls.getpeercert()
        version = tls.version()
expires = datetime.fromtimestamp(ssl.cert_time_to_seconds(cert["notAfter"]), tz=timezone.utc)
subject = dict(item[0] for item in cert["subject"])
print(f"{host}: {version}, subject CN={subject.get('commonName')}")
print(f"expires {expires:%Y-%m-%d} ({(expires - datetime.now(timezone.utc)).days} days left)")

blocks.syntax: ctx = ssl.create_default_context();  tls = ctx.wrap_socket(sock, server_hostname=name);  tls.getpeercert()

how.text: `wrap_socket` performs the TLS handshake on an already connected socket. `getpeercert()` returns a dict for a verified certificate with keys such as `subject`, `issuer`, `notBefore`, `notAfter` and `subjectAltName`. `ssl.cert_time_to_seconds()` converts the date strings. `tls.version()` and `tls.cipher()` report what was negotiated.

blocks.text: Driving other programs with subprocess

Python can use the tools you already know. `subprocess.run` is covered in [Files and pipelines](#py-files); the rules that matter here are to pass a **list** of arguments (no shell, so no injection), set `timeout`, and parse text defensively.
The part worth practicing in the page is the parsing. This block takes macOS `ping` summary text and extracts numbers with `re`:

import re

text = """--- example.com ping statistics ---
10 packets transmitted, 9 packets received, 10.0% packet loss
round-trip min/avg/max/stddev = 11.221/12.804/15.032/1.611 ms
"""
sent, got = map(int, re.search(r"(\d+) packets transmitted, (\d+) packets received", text).groups())
lo, avg, hi = map(float, re.search(r"= ([\d.]+)/([\d.]+)/([\d.]+)", text).groups())

blocks.text: Linux prints `10 packets transmitted, 9 received` (no word "packets" after the count) and `rtt min/avg/max/mdev`. The `netkit` capstone handles both with an optional group. Portable parsing means testing against text from every platform you care about, and saving samples as test fixtures.
A ping sweeper runs `ping -c 1` against every host of a network in parallel threads (each thread waits on a child process, so threads suit this too). Create `sweep.py`:

blocks.code:
import ipaddress
import subprocess
import sys
from concurrent.futures import ThreadPoolExecutor

# macOS: -W is milliseconds. Linux: -W is seconds.
WAIT = "1000" if sys.platform == "darwin" else "1"

def alive(ip):
    r = subprocess.run(["ping", "-c", "1", "-W", WAIT, str(ip)],
                       capture_output=True, text=True, timeout=5)
    return ip if r.returncode == 0 else None

net = ipaddress.ip_network(sys.argv[1] if len(sys.argv) > 1 else "192.168.1.0/24")
if net.num_addresses > 1024 or not net.is_private:
    sys.exit("sweep: private networks up to /22 only")
with ThreadPoolExecutor(max_workers=64) as pool:
    for ip in filter(None, pool.map(alive, net.hosts())):
        print(ip)

blocks.text: macOS `ping -W` takes **milliseconds**; Linux takes seconds. The script picks the right value with `sys.platform`. This is the sort of portability trap that makes parsing and flags worth testing on both systems.

blocks.title: Sweep results depend on who answers

blocks.text: Hosts that block ICMP, and phones that sleep their Wi-Fi radio, do not reply and so look absent. `arp -a` right after a sweep lists neighbours that answered ARP even if they ignore ping.

The same pattern drives `dig` for a bulk resolver, but `socket.getaddrinfo` gives you the system's own view without a child process. This version resolves a list of names in parallel and prints them in input order. Create `bulkdns.py`:

import socket

from concurrent.futures import ThreadPoolExecutor, as_completed

def resolve(name):
    try:
        infos = socket.getaddrinfo(name, None, proto=socket.IPPROTO_TCP)
        return name, sorted({i[4][0] for i in infos}), None
    except socket.gaierror as exc:
        return name, [], exc.strerror

names = [ln.strip() for ln in sys.stdin if ln.strip()]
with ThreadPoolExecutor(max_workers=16) as pool:
    futures = [pool.submit(resolve, n) for n in names]
    results = {}
    for fut in as_completed(futures):
        name, addrs, err = fut.result()
        results[name] = (addrs, err)

for name in names:                       # print in input order
    addrs, err = results[name]
    print(f"{name:<24} {', '.join(addrs) if addrs else 'FAILED: ' + err}")

A simple uptime monitor
A monitor is a loop with state. This one checks whether a TCP port accepts connections, times the connect, and prints a line when the state changes. Create `uptime_monitor.py`:

If you pipe it, add `flush=True` to the prints or run `python3 -u`, because Python buffers stdout when it is not a terminal.
select, selectors and asyncio

Threads cost memory and need locks. A different model handles many sockets in **one thread**: ask the kernel which sockets are ready (`select`, or on macOS `kqueue` through the `selectors` module), then read only from those. `asyncio` builds a friendlier layer on that idea: functions defined with `async def` pause at `await` and let other tasks run.

blocks.name: asyncio.open_connection()
blocks.sum: Open a TCP connection inside an async program and get a reader and a writer.
blocks.syntax: reader, writer = await asyncio.open_connection(host, port);  await asyncio.wait_for(coro, timeout);  await asyncio.gather(*coros);  asyncio.run(main())

how.text: Each `await` is a point where the task yields while the kernel works. `gather` runs many coroutines at once and returns results in order. `wait_for` cancels the inner call and raises `TimeoutError` after the deadline. `asyncio.start_server(handler, host, port)` is the server side; the handler receives `(reader, writer)`. A single thread can hold thousands of connections, and there are no data races between awaits.

examples.desc: Check three ports concurrently
examples.code: python3 async_check.py 127.0.0.1 7990 9010

examples.desc: Print one open port per line
examples.code: python3 async_check.py 127.0.0.1 7990 9010 | tr -d '[],' | tr ' ' '\n' | tail -n +2

gotchas: Any blocking call inside a coroutine (`time.sleep`, `requests.get`, `socket.recv` on a blocking socket) freezes every task. Use `await asyncio.sleep`, async libraries, or `asyncio.to_thread()`.

blocks.text: The asyncio version of a connect check, `async_check.py`:

blocks.code:
import asyncio
import sys

async def check(host, port, timeout=1.0):
    try:
        reader, writer = await asyncio.wait_for(asyncio.open_connection(host, port), timeout)
    except (OSError, asyncio.TimeoutError):
        return port, False
    writer.close()
    await writer.wait_closed()
    return port, True

async def main(host, ports):
    results = await asyncio.gather(*(check(host, p) for p in ports))
    print("open:", [p for p, ok in results if ok])

asyncio.run(main(sys.argv[1], range(int(sys.argv[2]), int(sys.argv[3]) + 1)))

blocks.text: Compare it with the thread pool version. Both finish in about one timeout. The asyncio version creates 1,000+ tasks without 1,000 threads, but note it still opens that many sockets at once, so it hits the same `ulimit -n` wall. Real code uses an `asyncio.Semaphore` to cap concurrency.
Packet crafting with scapy

Sockets give you TCP and UDP payloads; the kernel writes the headers. To craft the headers yourself, or to read raw packets, you need a **raw socket** or a library. `scapy` builds packets by stacking layers with `/` and sends them with `sr1` (send, receive one answer) or captures them with `sniff`. It needs root, because raw packet access is privileged. Install it in a virtual environment, and use it on your own network only.

See [What next](#next) for where scapy leads.

`sudo python3 script.py` uses root's `PATH` and may pick a different interpreter that lacks your packages. Call the venv's Python by path, and read the script before running anything as root. Root plus a typo in a packet loop can flood your own network.

blocks.title: Address already in use

task.text: Break it on purpose. Start `echo_server.py` in tab 1. In tab 2 start it a second time and read the error. Then find the process that owns port 9000 with `lsof` and stop it, and start the server again. Finally explain, in one sentence, why `SO_REUSEADDR` would **not** have prevented that first error.

hints: `kill` takes the PID; `kill $(lsof -tiTCP:9000 -sTCP:LISTEN)` does both steps.
blocks.solution:
python3 echo_server.py &
python3 echo_server.py        # OSError: [Errno 48] Address already in use
kill $(lsof -tiTCP:9000 -sTCP:LISTEN)
python3 echo_server.py

why.text: A live listener owns the port, and `SO_REUSEADDR` does not allow two listeners. It only helps when the previous owner has gone and its closed connections are lingering in TIME_WAIT.

task.text: Write `parse_ports(spec)` that expands a spec such as `"80,443,8000-8003"` into a sorted list of unique integers. Raise `ValueError` for a port below 1 or above 65535, and for a reversed range like `"9-3"`.

blocks.title: Decode a TCP header

task.text: Write `describe_tcp(hexstr)` that takes the 20-byte TCP header as a hex string and returns a string like `"50085 -> 80 SYN"`. The flag names, low bit first, are FIN, SYN, RST, PSH, ACK, URG; join several set flags with `"|"`. Fields: `!HHIIHHHH` gives source port, destination port, sequence, acknowledgment, offset and flags word, window, checksum, urgent.

blocks.solution:
import struct

def describe_tcp(hexstr):
    sport, dport, seq, ack, word, win, csum, urg = struct.unpack("!HHIIHHHH", bytes.fromhex(hexstr))
    names = ["FIN", "SYN", "RST", "PSH", "ACK", "URG"]
    flags = "|".join(n for i, n in enumerate(names) if word & (1 << i))
    return f"{sport} -> {dport} {flags}"

why.text: The flags are single bits in the low byte of the offset/flags word, so a mask with `1 << i` tests each. A SYN+ACK from a server is the second packet of the handshake you saw in the `handshake` widget.

task.text: Start `echo_server.py`, `api_server.py` and `python3 -m http.server 8000 --bind 127.0.0.1` in three tabs. In a fourth, run your `portscan.py` (project below) over `8000-9100` and compare its list with what `lsof -nP -iTCP -sTCP:LISTEN` shows. Both lists should agree.

blocks.title: Frame it

task.text: The chat server splits messages on `\n`. A user pastes text containing a newline into `nc`. What does the server do with it, and what would you change in the protocol to allow multi-line messages? Name one real protocol that uses each of the two framing strategies from this chapter.

blocks.solution: The server sees two separate lines and broadcasts two chat messages. To allow multi-line messages, switch to length-prefixed frames (`!H` length, then payload) or escape the newline. Delimiter framing: HTTP headers, SMTP, IRC. Length prefix: DNS over TCP, TLS records.

why.text: Framing is a protocol decision. Delimiters are easy to read and debug by hand, but the payload may never contain the delimiter. Length prefixes allow any bytes, but need exact bookkeeping and a limit to stop a hostile length like 4 GB.

questions.q: A TCP `recv(4096)` returns `b""`. What does that mean?

options.text: The peer closed its sending side

questions.why: An empty bytes object signals end of stream. A timeout raises `TimeoutError`, and with no data available a blocking `recv` simply waits.

questions.q: A client calls `sendall(b"A")` then `sendall(b"B")`. The server calls `recv` twice. What is guaranteed?

options.text: The bytes arrive in order, but may be split or merged into any chunks

questions.why: TCP preserves byte order and content, not send boundaries. Merge or split is normal, so protocols need framing.

questions.q: Which `struct` format character at the start selects network byte order?
questions.why: `!` (and `>`) mean big-endian, the order used on the wire. `<` is little-endian.

questions.q: What does `connect_ex` return for a closed local port?

options.text: A non-zero errno such as 61 on macOS

questions.why: `connect_ex` returns the error number instead of raising. Zero means the connection succeeded.

questions.q: Why are threads a good fit for a port scanner despite the GIL?

options.text: The GIL does not exist in Python 3
Threads blocked in socket calls release the GIL, so the waiting overlaps
Each thread runs on its own CPU in parallel Python code

questions.why: The scanner is I/O-bound. While one thread waits on a connect timeout, others run. CPU-bound Python code would not speed up this way.

questions.q: Which target is acceptable for `portscan.py` without any permission question?

options.text: A server you found on a list of open ports online
Any host whose owner "would not mind"

questions.why: Loopback is your own machine. For anything else you need ownership or explicit permission, and `scanme.nmap.org` is the standard example of a published permission.

blocks.text: Project: portscan.py

Build the scanner that `netkit scan` reuses in the capstone. It resolves the host, refuses anything that is not loopback, private or link-local, tests every port with a connect timeout in a thread pool, and prints either a readable list or JSON. The exit status tells scripts what happened: 0 open ports found, 1 none found, 2 bad usage or refused target.

This tool opens a TCP connection to each port you list. Run it against `127.0.0.1`, your own devices, and your own LAN. The address guard exists to stop mistakes such as a typo or a name that resolves to a public server. Do not edit it out. If you later need to scan a host that you have written permission to test, add an explicit `--i-have-permission` flag and log each use rather than removing the check.
Step 1: Create the file

Make it executable: `chmod +x portscan.py`. Read it once before running. Note three decisions: `connect_ex` instead of exceptions keeps the probe tiny; `pool.map` keeps results in port order; and the address check happens after name resolution, so a name that points to a public address is refused too.
Step 2: Run it against yourself
Start something to find: `python3 -m http.server 8000 --bind 127.0.0.1 &` and `python3 echo_server.py &`.

blocks.code:
$ ./portscan.py 127.0.0.1 -p 8000-9100
Scanned 1101 ports on 127.0.0.1 (127.0.0.1)
   8000/tcp  open  irdmi
   9000/tcp  open  cslistener
$ echo $?
0
$ ./portscan.py localhost -p 9000,9001 --json
{"host": "localhost", "address": "127.0.0.1", "scanned": 2, "open": [9000]}
$ ./portscan.py 93.184.216.34
portscan: refusing 93.184.216.34: not loopback or private. Scan only what you own or have permission to test.
$ echo $?
2

blocks.text: `getservbyport` reads the system services database (`/etc/services`). macOS ships the full IANA list, so even 8000 and 9000 get registered names (`irdmi`, `cslistener`) that say nothing about what actually listens there; only ports missing from the file print `unknown`.
Step 3: Use it in a pipeline
The JSON mode feeds other tools. This lists only the open ports of your Mac, one per line, ready for a loop:

blocks.code: ./portscan.py 127.0.0.1 -p 1-10000 --json | jq -r '.open[]'

blocks.text: Combine it with your sweeper to scan every live host on your LAN, still only your own network:

blocks.code:
python3 sweep.py 192.168.1.0/24 | while read -r ip; do
  echo "== $ip"; ./portscan.py "$ip" -p 22,80,443,445,8080 --timeout 1
done
